text: , and socio-eco- nomic factors, as well as the effects of antiepileptic drugs.1-3,5-7,10-12 A single generalised seizure does not usually pose clinical problems for the fetus, but both mother and fetus are at risk of serious trauma from maternal falls, and intra-uterine deaths have been reported. It is widely considered that sta- tus epilepticus is associated with significant mortality in mother and fetus. The frequency of seizures may increase during pregnancy in some women; this might be related to hormonal or other factors such as lack of sleep, but one of the main reasons is likely to be decreased plasma-antiepileptic concentrations due to changes in drug clearance and binding as pregnancy progresses (and some13,14 have recommended therapeutic drug monitoring in at-risk patients). However, analysis15 of 1956 pregnancies of 1882 epileptic women recorded in an international antiepileptic drugs and pregnancy registry (EURAP) found that 58.3% were seizure-free throughout pregnancy. Seizures occurred during delivery in 3.5%, most commonly in those who had seizures earlier during pregnancy, and status epilepticus occurred in 1.8%, with one case of still-birth and none of miscarriage or maternal mortality. The authors noted that publication bias favoured the reporting of adverse outcomes in pregnancy. As with many other aspects of epilepsy, it is difficult to disentangle the potential adverse effects of therapy from those of the disease. However, although the risk of major malformations such as congenital heart defects, neural tube defects, urogenital defects, and orofacial clefts is somewhat increased in offspring of all women with epilep- sy,3,7 there is clear evidence that in children of women treated with antiepileptic drugs it is 2 to 3 times that in the general population, and the risk is higher in women taking multiple drugs or in those who take antiepileptics during the first trimester.7 Despite this, evidence linking specific drugs with particu- lar patterns of malformation is limited and often unclear. There appears to be strong evidence for a dose-related in- creased risk of major malformation with val- proate,7,10-12,16-20 and increased risk has been reported for carbamazepine, phenobarbital, and primidone.7,10,11 The rate of major abnormality with phenytoin does not seem to be higher than in the general population.7 However, a well established fetal antiepileptic syndrome (FAS) has been reported with phenytoin, as with other antiepileptic drugs,6 including some older drugs such as trimethadione. Al- though early reports associated syndromes with specific drugs, such as fetal hydantoin syndrome (phenytoin), or fetal valproate syndrome, there is considerable overlap in the reported effects and recent reviews consider these as manifestations of a single condition, FAS.6,11 The dysmor- phic facial changes characteristic
